lines: I.  Introduction

Fig. 1.  The upgrade erases a learned fleet's benefit. Against its own base driver the fleet saves fuel under fixed-time signals (blue). Under a learned signal without timing it is its base driver (grey, zero by construction); with the old timing served as SPaT it loses fuel and time (orange).

Traffic signals and connected fleets are both becoming learned policies, owned by different parties and upgraded on different schedules. A fleet trained under fixed-time signals reads the broadcast signal phase and timing (SPaT) as a plan; a learned signal re-decides every few seconds, and the plan is gone.

In SUMO on a 16-signal grid, a PPO eco-driving fleet saves 6.5% fuel against its base driver under fixed-time control. After the signals are upgraded the benefit is gone. Withholding the timing turns the fleet back into its base driver; publishing a forecast of the learned signal costs the fleet's own vehicles time; and making the signal commit, abstain or follow a predictable split never met the limits.

Nothing in the fleet's own inputs announces the failure: an upgrade can leave every statistic of what the fleet observes unchanged while its trained rule becomes more than ten times worse than the best rule (a machine-checked example). Retraining is the usual remedy, but the two owners rarely retrain together. Here both learned policies stay frozen, and only the two interfaces between them change: what the fleet is told, and what the signal counts.
Related Work

SPaT prediction for adaptive signals [1, 2] and GLOSA at highly adaptive lights [3] improve the forecast alone; eco-driving under uncertain or actuated timing [4, 5] changes the vehicle; joint control and FoRL [6], which trains a signal to forecast and keep its own actions, retrain one side. Observation adapters for a frozen policy, such as DC-Ada [7], learn a transform by reward-only search.

A forecast that changes the behaviour it predicts is the consistency problem of anticipatory route guidance [8] and of performative prediction [9]. Here it appears at the signal–eco-driving interface, where the fleet's reaction passes through a learned signal's input.
II.  Methodology

Fig. 2.  The closed loop and the two interfaces TSI changes (blue). Published timing makes agents glide; a halting-count signal stops seeing them, holds its green, and the forecast's own target moves (orange).

Four registered stages: M1, a fleet worth protecting; M2, the upgrade removes its benefit, measured as a difference in differences against the base driver σ*; M3, a repair through the interfaces alone; M4, transfer to new traffic, new policies and new networks. Each experiment's protocol was written before its code ran.

FLEET SIDE. A hybrid provider answers exactly when the timing is determined (a yellow whose next green serves the link) and otherwise with a state-conditioned quantile forecaster, fitted to eight logged episodes of the deployed signal with a query-weighted pinball loss:

LIGHT SIDE. A speed-binned count in front of the frozen signal's halting-count input adds slowly approaching vehicles. A = B = 0 is the deployed signal; (A, B) is chosen per signal on tuning traffic. Calibration costs 52 simulated episodes per signal and no gradient step for either policy.

DECISION. Half the vehicles are fleet agents. A repair passes only if fleet fuel falls and every time loss (city, fleet, human) stays below +0.5 s/veh at the one-sided upper bound of a crossed bootstrap over signal, fleet and traffic seeds, with no more teleports or unfinished trips:
II.  Methodology, continued

WHY ONE SIDE CANNOT SUFFICE. A threshold signal serves an approach when its perceived demand reaches θ. If a fleet share ρ glides and the input weights a glider by A, a forecast learned without the fleet errs by

The forecast stays true only when the signal counts a glider as a halted car (A = 1). With a halting count it is self-defeating, the more so the larger the fleet, and with n vehicles the signal misses its demand with probability at least pⁿ. In a one-car model each one-sided repair provably fails and the two together reach the optimum. Machine-checked in Lean 4: four modules, 32 declarations, standard axioms only.

The model fixes the sign of every measured change in green time: longer under the service for the halting-count signal (grid4 15.0 → 17.1 s; one-lane spider 18.9 → 28.7 s), none for MaxPressure, which counts every speed (18.1 → 18.0 s), and none under TSI on grid4 (15.0 s).
III.  Results
Fig. 3.  TSI against the no-SPaT fallback in every registered test (95% intervals; verdicts at each test's level).

ABOUT THREE-FIFTHS OF THE BENEFIT COMES BACK. Registered confirmation: −3.85% fleet fuel (95% CI −4.43 to −3.26), every time loss within the limit. It repeated on two further traffic panels (−3.70%, −3.85%) and on two independently retrained sets of signals and fleets, recalibrated from scratch (−2.61%, −2.97%). The service alone and the adapter alone each failed in every ablation.
ONE SETTING SERVES EVERY SIGNAL. (A, B) = (1, 0.5), fixed in advance, met every limit on unseen policies (−2.88%), so no per-site search is needed.

THE ALTERNATIVES COST TIME. A corrected DC-Ada port tuned at TSI's budget saves similar fuel (−3.45%) but adds 2.87 s/veh to the fleet's time loss and fails; with four times the budget it does worse (−0.83%, +3.44 s/veh). Against retraining the fleet no fuel difference was detected and TSI's time losses are lower, but fuel non-inferiority at 0.5 pp was not shown.
IV.  Discussion

Fig. 4.  Mechanism. Under the service the learned signal holds its greens longer (A); the fleet's extra time grows with that lengthening (B); on a replayed schedule exact timing saves both fuel and time (C).

A PREDICTION MADE BEFORE THE RUN HELD. With MaxPressure, whose input counts vehicles at every speed, the theory says no light-side change is needed: the fleet-side service alone met every limit (−2.68%) and the greens did not lengthen.

WHERE IT STOPS. On one-lane spider TSI failed four registered attempts. Exact accounting of the answers actually served shows publication shifts the forecast by +7.8 s and commanded agents hold five times as many human followers as on grid4. A refitted forecaster removes the shift but not the failure; the same network with two lanes passes (−1.49%). On rand3, harder to forecast, a wider adapter range passes (−2.17%).
Within the limits at 80% detection, 1 m/s speed noise and 20% message loss; a 1-s SPaT latency cuts the saving to 0.74%.
Limitations

Simulation only, on three synthetic networks. The saving under learned signals holds with HBEFA4 but becomes a 1.76% increase with PHEMlight5 on identical trajectories; the frozen design does not survive IDM drivers.
Fails on one-lane roads with enough following traffic; needs logs of each deployed signal; the theory fixes signs, not magnitudes.
V.  Conclusions

When one learned population is upgraded, a working pair can fail without either one's inputs looking unusual. Neither interface alone repairs it; together they bring back about three-fifths of the fleet's benefit with both policies frozen.
Before upgrading signals a learned fleet relies on, two questions matter: does the signal's input see the fleet's slower approach, and can followers pass a slow agent?
